q: You enable the storage account firewall and add VNet1/SubnetA. VMs in SubnetA still cannot reach the storage account. The most likely missing step is:
opts: The Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on SubnetA
An NSG rule on SubnetA allowing inbound port 445
A public IP on each VM
exp: A storage firewall rule for a VNet subnet only works if that subnet has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint, so traffic arrives with the subnet's identity. Without it, the VMs' traffic comes from a public IP and is blocked. A private endpoint is a different approach, port 445 is only for SMB, and public IPs aren't needed.

q: After enabling the storage firewall with 'selected networks', Azure Backup and some Microsoft services stop working. Which setting fixes this without opening the account to the internet?
opts: Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account
Add 0.0.0.0/0 to the IP rules and require secure transfer
exp: 'Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account' is an exception in the storage firewall. Services such as Azure Backup, Azure Site Recovery and Azure Monitor can still reach the account even when only selected networks are allowed. Adding 0.0.0.0/0 or disabling the firewall would open the account to the whole internet, and anonymous access is about unauthenticated reads, not network rules.

q: You administer the storage account from your office (public IP 203.0.113.10) while the firewall is enabled. What do you add?
opts: A VNet rule for your office with the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint
Your office public IP (or range) to the firewall's IP address rules
A private endpoint at the office
exp: The storage firewall has two kinds of rules: IP rules for public internet addresses and ranges, and virtual network rules for Azure subnets. Your office reaches Azure from its public IP, so add 203.0.113.10 as an IP rule. A VNet rule only works for Azure subnets, a private endpoint lives in an Azure VNet, and NSG rules don't control access to a storage account.

q: Which SAS fields limit a token so that it works only from a given IP range and only over HTTPS?
exp: A SAS token can carry sip (signed IP — the allowed address or range) and spr (signed protocol — https, or https,http). With sip and spr=https, the token only works from that range and only over HTTPS. 'Signed services' chooses blob, file, queue or table; the policy name and the access tier don't restrict callers.

q: You issued ad-hoc service SAS tokens valid for 1 year. One token leaked. How do you revoke it?
opts: Regenerate the account key that signed it
Remove the user from Entra ID
Set the blob tier to Archive
exp: An ad-hoc SAS can't be revoked individually; regenerating the signing key kills it (and all others signed with that key). Use stored access policies to avoid this.

q: What is the main benefit of creating SAS tokens from a stored access policy?
opts: You can modify or revoke the policy afterwards, which immediately affects all SAS tied to it
Tokens bypass the storage firewall, so partners need no IP rule or private endpoint of their own
exp: A SAS linked to a stored access policy takes its start time, expiry and permissions from the policy. Change the policy, or delete it, and every SAS that uses it is updated or revoked at once, without rotating account keys. Policy-based SAS still expire, still need a signature, and still obey the firewall.

q: How many stored access policies can you define per container?
exp: Each container, file share, queue or table can hold at most 5 stored access policies. To revoke SAS tokens linked to a policy you change or delete that policy, so plan the five slots carefully, for example one per partner or purpose.

q: Which SAS type is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the storage account key?
exp: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key that you request using Microsoft Entra credentials, not with the account key. That's why Microsoft recommends it: no account key is involved, and access is tied to an identity with RBAC permissions. Account and service SAS are both signed with the account key.

q: According to current Microsoft Learn documentation, which services support a user delegation SAS?
opts: Blob (including Data Lake), Queue, Table and Azure Files
Queue and Table only, when the account is general-purpose v2
exp: A user delegation SAS is supported for Blob storage (including Data Lake), Queue, Table and Azure Files. Older study material says Blob only, because support for the other services was added later.

q: How many access keys does a storage account have, and why?
opts: 2, so you can rotate one key while clients use the other
3, so primary, secondary and tertiary regions each have their own
exp: Each storage account has two access keys (key1 and key2) so you can rotate them without downtime: move applications to key2, regenerate key1, move them back to the new key1, then regenerate key2. With only one key, regenerating it would immediately break every client.

q: Which service stores storage keys securely for applications and can help automate rotation?
exp: Azure Key Vault stores secrets such as storage account keys securely and can manage their rotation. On the storage account, a key expiration policy reminds you when keys are due for rotation. Advisor, Monitor and Network Watcher don't store secrets.

q: Azure file share users must authenticate with their on-premises AD DS identities over SMB. Besides enabling AD DS authentication on the account, what must be configured for users to access files?
opts: Share-level RBAC permissions AND NTFS permissions on files and directories
A SAS token per user AND anonymous read access on the root directory of the share
exp: Identity-based access to Azure Files has two layers, and a user needs both. Share-level permission is an Azure RBAC role on the share, such as Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor. File- and folder-level permission is Windows NTFS ACLs, checked when they open files. SAS tokens can't be used to mount SMB shares, and anonymous access isn't supported for Azure Files.

q: Which THREE identity sources are supported for Azure Files SMB identity-based authentication?
exp: Azure Files supports three identity sources for SMB: on-premises AD DS (the account is joined to your domain), Microsoft Entra Domain Services (a managed domain in Azure), and Microsoft Entra Kerberos (for hybrid identities, without domain controllers being reachable). Google identities and local Windows accounts can't be used.

q: Which built-in role allows reading blob data using Entra ID authentication, without granting account management rights?
exp: Storage Blob Data Reader is a data-plane role: it allows reading containers and blobs with Microsoft Entra authentication, and nothing else. Reader and Storage Account Contributor are control-plane roles: they cover the account's settings, not the data. Contributor manages the account and can read data only by fetching the access keys.

q: A user with the Reader role on a storage account browses blobs in the portal using 'Microsoft Entra user account' authentication. What happens?
opts: Full blob read access, because Reader includes every read data action
Access denied to blob data, because Reader is a control-plane role
exp: Reader is a control-plane role: it can see the storage account and its settings but grants no permission to read the data. When the portal uses 'Microsoft Entra user account' authentication, reading blobs needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader, so access is denied. (With access-key mode it would also fail, because Reader can't list the keys.)

q: To let anyone on the internet read blobs by URL without listing the container, set the container's anonymous access level to:
exp: The 'Blob' anonymous access level lets anyone read a blob if they know its URL, but they can't list the container's contents. 'Container' allows reading and listing. 'Private' allows no anonymous access, and 'Public-All' doesn't exist. Anonymous access must also be allowed at the account level.

q: Answer Yes or No to each statement:
stmts: Regenerating an account key invalidates every SAS signed with it
A SAS can grant more permissions than the stored access policy it references
Unless exceptions are configured, the storage firewall applies to all networks, including Azure services
Entra ID authentication is supported for Blob and Queue data operations
exp: Regenerating an account key invalidates every SAS signed with that key. A SAS can't grant more than the stored access policy it references. Unless you add exceptions, the storage firewall blocks all networks, Azure services included. And Entra ID authentication works for Blob and Queue data operations.

q: Which storage account type should you create for general scenarios that need blobs, files, queues, and tables with all redundancy options?
exp: General-purpose v2 (GPv2) supports blobs, files, queues and tables, the hot, cool, cold and archive tiers, and every redundancy option (LRS, ZRS, GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS). It's Microsoft's recommended default. Premium accounts support only one service each and fewer redundancy options, and BlobStorage is a legacy kind.

q: You need the lowest latency for an SMB file share used by a database workload. Which account kind?
exp: Premium file shares run on FileStorage accounts, which use SSDs for low latency and high IOPS — what database workloads on SMB need. Standard GPv2 shares use HDD-based storage. BlockBlobStorage is premium for blobs, not file shares, and GPv1 is a legacy kind.

q: Which redundancy option keeps three copies of data within a single datacenter only?
exp: Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps three synchronous copies inside a single datacenter in one region. It protects against disk or rack failures but not against losing the whole datacenter. ZRS spreads the copies across zones, and GRS and GZRS also copy data to another region.

q: Data must survive a full region outage AND the app must be able to read from the secondary region at any time. Minimum redundancy?
exp: GRS and RA-GRS both copy data asynchronously to the paired region, so it survives a region outage. Only the read-access versions (RA-GRS and RA-GZRS) let applications read the secondary copy at any time, through the -secondary endpoint. With plain GRS the secondary can only be read after a failover. LRS and ZRS stay in one region.

q: Which redundancy option replicates synchronously across three availability zones in the primary region AND asynchronously to a secondary region?
exp: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) stores three copies across availability zones in the primary region (like ZRS) and also copies the data asynchronously to the secondary region (like GRS). ZRS stays in one region, GRS uses only one datacenter in the primary region, and RA-LRS doesn't exist.

q: During a prolonged primary-region outage on a GRS account, who can initiate the failover, and what is the redundancy afterwards?
opts: Only Microsoft can initiate it; the account stays GRS with the regions swapped
The customer can initiate it; the account becomes LRS in the new primary region
exp: With customer-managed failover, you can start the failover yourself without waiting for Microsoft. After an unplanned failover, the old secondary becomes the primary and the account is LRS there. You then reconfigure geo-redundancy to protect it again.

q: Which redundancy options can a Premium (block blob / file) storage account use?
exp: Premium storage accounts (block blob and file shares) support only LRS and, in regions that offer it, ZRS. They have no geo-redundant options such as GRS or RA-GRS, so for protection against a region outage you need another approach, such as object replication or copying data to a standard account.

q: Object replication between two storage accounts requires which prerequisites?
opts: Blob versioning on source and destination, and change feed on the source
Blob soft delete on source and destination, and a lifecycle rule
Both accounts in the same region
exp: Object replication works from the blob version history and the change log. The source and destination accounts must both have blob versioning turned on, and the source must have change feed enabled. The accounts can be in different regions or subscriptions, and soft delete isn't required.

q: Which statement best describes object replication?
opts: Synchronous copy of all blob types, including page and append blobs, inside the same Azure region
Asynchronous copy of block blobs between accounts, which can be in different regions or subscriptions
exp: Object replication copies block blobs asynchronously from a container in one account to a container in another account. The accounts can be in different regions, subscriptions or even tenants. It isn't synchronous, doesn't support page or append blobs, and archived blobs aren't replicated.

q: Azure Storage service-side encryption at rest is:
opts: Always enabled and cannot be disabled
exp: Azure Storage always encrypts data at rest with 256-bit AES (server-side encryption). It's on by default for every account and can't be turned off. You can choose who manages the key — Microsoft or you (customer-managed keys) — but not whether data is encrypted.

q: To use customer-managed keys for a storage account, the key vault must have which two protections enabled?
exp: When a storage account uses a customer-managed key, losing that key would make the data unreadable forever. Azure therefore requires the key vault to have soft delete and purge protection enabled, so a deleted key can be recovered and can't be purged immediately. Firewalls, tags and HSMs are optional.

q: Infrastructure (double) encryption for a storage account can be enabled:
opts: Any time in the Encryption blade
exp: Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer of encryption at the infrastructure level with a different key. It can only be chosen when the storage account is created and can't be turned on afterwards; to get it, create a new account and move the data.

q: Which AzCopy command uploads C:\data to a container and copies only files that changed since last time?
exp: azcopy sync compares the source and destination (by last-modified time) and copies only new or changed files, so repeated runs transfer just the differences. azcopy copy copies everything you give it, azcopy move isn't for incremental sync, and benchmark only tests performance.

q: AzCopy can authenticate to Blob storage using:
opts: Entra ID (azcopy login) or SAS tokens
The account name and an SSH key pair
exp: AzCopy can authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID (azcopy login, which also supports managed identities and service principals — you need a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor) or with a SAS token appended to the URL. It doesn't use SSH keys or an account name alone.

q: Azure Storage Explorer is best described as:
opts: A web-only monitoring dashboard that shows storage capacity, latency, and availability
A free cross-platform desktop app to manage blobs, files, queues, tables, and Data Lake
exp: Azure Storage Explorer is a free desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux. You can browse and manage blobs, files, queues, tables and Data Lake storage across several accounts and subscriptions, upload and download data, and manage SAS and access policies. It isn't a web dashboard or a PowerShell module.

q: You must copy 60 TB of data to Azure from a site with very low bandwidth. The practical option is:
opts: AzCopy with parallel uploads over the weekend
Azure Import/Export or Azure Data Box
RDP file copy to a VM
exp: 60 TB over a very slow link could take weeks or months. Azure Data Box (or the Import/Export service with your own disks) is an offline transfer: you copy the data to a device on site and ship it to an Azure datacenter, where it's uploaded. AzCopy, Storage Explorer and RDP copies all depend on the network.

q: Answer Yes or No to each statement:
stmts: A storage account name must be globally unique, 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only
You can change LRS to GRS on a standard GPv2 account without recreating it
A storage account can be moved to another resource group
The account's default access tier applies to Azure file shares
exp: Storage account names must be globally unique, 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only. You can change a standard GPv2 account from LRS to GRS in place, and you can move the account to another resource group. The default access tier applies to blobs only, not to Azure file shares, which have their own tiers.

q: Azure Files SMB shares use which port, which many ISPs block?
exp: SMB uses TCP port 445. Many ISPs and home routers block outbound 445 for security reasons, so mounting an Azure file share directly from home often fails with 'System error 53'. HTTP uses 80, HTTPS uses 443 and RDP uses 3389.

q: On-premises users can't reach an SMB file share because the ISP blocks port 445. What's a practical solution?
opts: Use VPN/ExpressRoute (or Azure File Sync) so SMB doesn't go directly over the internet
Switch the account to RA-GRS so that users mount the share from the secondary region
exp: If the ISP blocks TCP 445, send SMB traffic through a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute (usually to a private endpoint), so it never travels directly over the internet. Alternatively, Azure File Sync caches the share on a local Windows Server that users reach on the LAN. Switching to HTTP or port 80 isn't possible for SMB, and redundancy settings don't affect connectivity.

q: Which file share protocol is available only on premium (FileStorage) accounts and is used from Linux?
exp: NFS 4.1 file shares are available only on premium FileStorage accounts and are mainly mounted from Linux clients. SMB 3.1.1 works on both standard and premium accounts. Azure Files doesn't offer FTP or WebDAV.

q: What is the correct hierarchy of Azure File Sync components?
opts: Storage Sync Service → sync group → one cloud endpoint + server endpoints
Storage Sync Service → server endpoint → many cloud endpoints per group
exp: Azure File Sync is built as a Storage Sync Service containing sync groups. Each sync group has exactly one cloud endpoint (an Azure file share) and one or more server endpoints (folders on registered Windows Servers). A Recovery Services vault isn't part of it.

q: What does cloud tiering in Azure File Sync do?
opts: Moves blobs to the archive tier
Keeps frequently used files on the local server while cold files become pointers, with full copies in Azure
Replicates all files in full between two local servers, while Azure keeps only their metadata
exp: Cloud tiering keeps frequently used files on the local server and replaces rarely used files with small pointers (reparse points), while the full copies stay in the Azure file share. When someone opens a tiered file, it's downloaded on demand. It doesn't compress files, change blob tiers or sync servers directly with each other.

q: Which blob type is used for virtual machine disks (VHDs)?
exp: Page blobs are made of 512-byte pages and support fast random reads and writes, which is how VM disks (VHDs) work. Block blobs suit files and objects that are uploaded whole, and append blobs suit logs that only grow at the end. There's no 'table blob'.

q: Which access tier is offline, so a blob can't be read until it's rehydrated?
exp: Archive is the only offline tier. You can't read or change an archived blob until you rehydrate it to hot, cool or cold, which can take up to 15 hours. Hot, cool and cold are online tiers with millisecond access.

q: Rehydrating an archived blob with Standard priority typically takes:
exp: Archived blobs are offline and must be rehydrated before you can read them. With Standard priority this can take up to 15 hours. High priority is faster — often under an hour for blobs smaller than 10 GB — but costs more.

q: What are the early-deletion periods for the cool, cold, and archive tiers?
exp: Each cooler tier has a minimum storage period: 30 days for cool, 90 days for cold and 180 days for archive. If you delete, overwrite or move a blob out earlier, you're charged for the rest of the period (prorated). Hot has no minimum.

q: Which tiers can be set as the default account-level access tier?
exp: A storage account's default access tier can be hot, cool or cold; new GPv2 accounts use hot unless you choose otherwise. Archive can only be set on individual blobs, never as the account default, because archived data is offline.

q: Blobs should move to cool after 30 days without modification, to archive after 90, and be deleted after 365. What do you configure?
opts: A lifecycle management policy with rules based on last modified time
An Azure Policy with a Modify effect that changes the access tier
exp: Blob lifecycle management lets you write rules such as 'tier to cool when last modified more than 30 days ago, to archive after 90 days, delete after 365 days', and Azure applies them automatically every day. Azure Policy governs resource settings, not data, and budgets and object replication don't move blobs between tiers.

q: After you create a new lifecycle management rule, roughly how long until its actions first run?
exp: After you create or change a lifecycle policy, it can take up to 24 hours to take effect, and the daily run itself can take more time to finish. So expect up to about 48 hours before blobs are first tiered or deleted.

q: What's the key difference between blob versioning and blob snapshots?
opts: Versioning creates a version automatically on every write or delete
Snapshots are created automatically on every write; versions are manual
exp: With versioning on, Azure automatically keeps the previous version every time a blob is overwritten or deleted, with no action from you. A snapshot is a read-only copy that you create yourself at a point in time. Both can restore earlier content, but only versioning does it automatically, and neither needs the archive tier.

q: Blob soft delete is set to 14 days. What does that mean?
opts: Deleted blobs can be undeleted within 14 days
Blobs can't be deleted for 14 days
The container is locked for 14 days
exp: Blob soft delete keeps a deleted (or overwritten) blob in a soft-deleted state for the retention period, here 14 days. You can undelete it during that time; afterwards it's permanently removed. It doesn't archive blobs, prevent deletion or lock the container.

q: Share snapshots for Azure Files are:
opts: Read-only point-in-time copies of the whole share, incremental in storage use
Full read-write copies of the whole share, billed at 100% each time
Automatic every hour and not configurable
exp: A share snapshot is a read-only point-in-time copy of the whole file share. Snapshots are incremental: only data changed since the previous snapshot is stored, so they're cheap. You take them manually or on a schedule with Azure Backup, and they work for SMB shares.

ctx: Invoices (block blobs) are stored in a GPv2 RA-GRS account. They must be instantly readable for 6 months and retained 7 years total. Instant access isn't needed after 6 months.
q: Which tier strategy is cheapest for months 7–84?
opts: Move to cool with a lifecycle rule and enable versioning
Move to archive with a lifecycle rule after 6 months
exp: Archive is the cheapest tier for data you must keep but rarely or never read, and instant access isn't needed after month 6. A lifecycle rule can move the invoices automatically after 6 months (archive has a 180-day minimum, which fits easily). Hot and cool cost much more per GB, and deleting would break the 7-year requirement.
